questiontext.text:
C6.Q1 — Definition and basic properties

\((F_N)_{kj}=\omega_N^{jk}/\sqrt N\) with \(\omega_N=e^{2\pi i/N}\). It is unitary, symmetric, and satisfies \(F_N^{4}=I\).

Write qft_matrix(n) returning the \(2^{n}\times2^{n}\) QFT matrix, and qft_apply(psi) applying it to a state vector whose length is a power of two.

qft_matrix(1)  ==  H
qft_apply(|0>^n)  ->  uniform superposition

testcode.text: import numpy as np H = np.array([[1,1],[1,-1]], dtype=complex)/np.sqrt(2) print(np.allclose(qft_matrix(1), H))
import numpy as np v = np.zeros(8, dtype=complex); v[0]=1 print(np.allclose(qft_apply(v), np.full(8, 1/np.sqrt(8))))
import numpy as np F = qft_matrix(3) print(np.allclose(F.conj().T @ F, np.eye(8)), np.allclose(F, F.T))
import numpy as np F = qft_matrix(2) print(np.allclose(np.linalg.matrix_power(F, 4), np.eye(4)))
import numpy as np rng = np.random.default_rng(1) v = rng.normal(size=16)+1j*rng.normal(size=16) ref = np.fft.ifft(v) * np.sqrt(16) print(np.allclose(qft_apply(v), ref))

name.text: C6.Q2 — The QFT circuit: Hadamards, controlled phases, SWAPs

questiontext.text:
C6.Q2 — Building the O(n^2) circuit

The product form of §1 becomes a circuit with \(n\) Hadamards, \(\binom{n}{2}\) controlled rotations \(R_m=\mathrm{diag}(1,e^{2\pi i/2^{m}})\), and a final qubit reversal.

Write qft_circuit_matrix(n) that constructs the QFT as a product of these elementary gates (do not return qft_matrix(n) directly) and returns the resulting \(2^{n}\times2^{n}\) matrix. Also write gate_count(n) returning the tuple (hadamards, controlled_rotations).

gate_count(4) -> (4, 6)
qft_circuit_matrix(3)  ==  qft_matrix(3)

testcode.text: import numpy as np U = qft_circuit_matrix(4) print(np.allclose(U.conj().T @ U, np.eye(16)))

questiontext.text:
C6.Q3 — Reading an eigenphase

With \(t\) ancillas, controlled powers of \(U\) followed by \(F^{\dagger}\) concentrate the ancilla register on the best \(t\)-bit approximation of \(\varphi\).

Write qpe_state(phi, t) returning the ancilla state \(\tfrac1{\sqrt{2^{t}}}\sum_y e^{2\pi i\varphi y}|y\rangle\) after applying the inverse QFT; qpe_probs(phi, t) returning the measurement distribution (rounded to 10 decimals); and qpe_estimate(phi, t) returning the most likely \(y/2^{t}\) as a float.

qpe_estimate(0.25, 3)  ->  0.25   (exact, 3 bits suffice)
qpe_estimate(0.3, 5)   ->  0.3125 (= 10/32, nearest 5-bit value)

name.text: C6.Q4 — The Hadamard test and the 4/pi^2 bound

questiontext.text:
C6.Q4 — One bit of phase per shot, and how many bits you really need

The Hadamard test measures \(\mathrm{Re}\langle u|U|u\rangle\); the accuracy theorem of §4 fixes the number of ancillas needed for \(n\)-bit precision at confidence \(1-\varepsilon\).

Write hadamard_test_p0(phi) returning \(\cos^{2}(\pi\varphi)\) rounded to 6 decimals; qpe_ancillas(n, eps) returning \(t=n+\lceil\log_2(2+\tfrac1{2\varepsilon})\rceil\) as an int; and success_prob(phi, t) returning the total probability that the measured \(y\) satisfies \(|y/2^{t}-\varphi|\le2^{-t}\) (taking the difference modulo 1), rounded to 6 decimals.

qpe_ancillas(4, 0.01) -> 4 + ceil(log2(52)) = 4 + 6 = 10
